import math
TITLE = 'Scholarship Centres in Mecca'
FROM_CITY = 'Umm Al-Qura University area, Mecca (reference)'
FROM_LAT = 21.3891
FROM_LON = 39.8579
MECCA_LAT = 21.4225
MECCA_LON = 39.8262
R = 6371.0
p1 = math.radians(FROM_LAT); p2 = math.radians(MECCA_LAT)
dp = math.radians(MECCA_LAT - FROM_LAT); dl = math.radians(MECCA_LON - FROM_LON)
a = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2
dist = 2*R*math.asin(math.sqrt(a))
y = math.sin(dl)*math.cos(p2); x = math.cos(p1)*math.sin(p2) - math.sin(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.cos(dl)
bearing = (math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x)) + 360) % 360
print('Place: ' + TITLE)
print('From: ' + FROM_CITY)
print('Great-circle distance to Mecca: %.1f km' % dist)
print('Initial bearing to Mecca: %.1f degrees' % bearing)
print('Method: haversine great-circle arithmetic on published coordinates; road distance differs.')

title: The Islamic Calendar and Mecca
description: The Islamic calendar is a lunar calendar of twelve months, beginning with Muharram and ending with Dhul-Hijjah, and Mecca's pilgrimage year is set by it: Hajj falls in Dhul-Hijjah, Ramadan is the ninth month, and the festivals of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha fall on the 1st of Shawwal and the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah respectively. Because the lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, Islamic months move through the solar seasons over about three decades, so the same Meccan festival falls in different seasons in different years. The start of each month depends on moon sighting and official announcement, so this record gives the calendar framework and its movement rule, and its demo converter is labelled as an arithmetic approximation, never as religious authority. This record is a fact record about a calendar system.

title: Ramadan in Mecca
description: Ramadan in Mecca is marked by fasting from dawn to sunset, by nightly Taraweeh prayers at the Grand Mosque, by iftar meals at sunset, and by a large increase in Umrah pilgrims, who come to Mecca in Ramadan in numbers that published descriptions describe as second only to Hajj. The Grand Mosque's Ramadan nights are among its most crowded, with prayers extending late into the night, and the last ten nights, including Laylat al-Qadr in tradition, draw still larger crowds. Published descriptions also note the provision of iftar meals and services for pilgrims and for the poor during the month. This record is a fact record about publicly observable practices and their scale; the spiritual significance of Ramadan is tradition, and the record presents it as tradition where it mentions it, without inventing doctrine about fasting rules, on which schools of thought differ in detail.

description: Teaching at the Grand Mosque takes place in circles and lessons in which scholars teach Quran, Hadith, jurisprudence, and Arabic to students and visitors, a practice published histories trace back centuries and published modern references describe as continuing today. Sermons, including the Friday sermon and the Arafat sermon during Hajj, are delivered publicly, and their content varies by occasion and by preacher, so this record gives no summary of any particular sermon as if it were permanent doctrine. title: Glossary: Tradition Terms
description: This glossary defines the tradition terms used across the Mecca scholarship and tradition pair, in plain language. The Quran is the central religious text of Islam. Hadith literature is the body of reports about sayings, actions, and approvals attributed to the Prophet. A school of thought, madhhab, is a jurisprudential tradition with its own methods. Ijtihad is independent legal reasoning by a qualified scholar, and a fatwa is a legal opinion given in answer to a question, which is not itself a law. Taraweeh is the nightly prayer performed in Ramadan, and Jumu'ah is the Friday congregational prayer. This record is a fact record of standard religious-studies usage, and where a term's meaning differs between schools, the glossary says traditions differ rather than giving one school's definition as universal.
